title: Dispute quality report
prompt: Before the monthly chargeback report, the disputes team checks every dispute record. Write `solve(disputes)` so it returns `dispute_id`, `status` and `quality` for every dispute.
rules: Check in this order and use the first problem found: `bad amount` (`disputed_amount` missing or not more than 0), `bad status` (`status` missing or not `open`, `won`, `lost` or `withdrawn`), `open but resolved` (status `open` with a `resolved_date`), `missing resolution` (any other status with no `resolved_date`), `resolved too early` (`resolved_date` before `opened_date`).
A dispute with none of these problems gets `valid`.
Return the three columns, in that order, for every dispute.
hints: Chain `F.when` in the rules' order and finish with `.otherwise("valid")`.
Write each `when` as a problem, and test for missing values with `isNull()`: a comparison with a missing value isn't true, so the row would slip through to `valid`.
By the time the open and missing-resolution checks run, the status is known to be one of the four, so `status == "open"` and `status != "open"` are safe there.
starter:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F


def solve(disputes):
    # Return dispute_id, status and quality for every dispute.
    return disputes
explanation: A `when` chain labels the first problem, and `otherwise` labels the rest: `F.when(F.col("disputed_amount").isNull() | (F.col("disputed_amount") <= 0), "bad amount").when(F.col("status").isNull() | ~F.col("status").isin("open", "won", "lost", "withdrawn"), "bad status").when((F.col("status") == "open") & F.col("resolved_date").isNotNull(), "open but resolved").when((F.col("status") != "open") & F.col("resolved_date").isNull(), "missing resolution").when(F.col("resolved_date") < F.col("opened_date"), "resolved too early").otherwise("valid")`. The `isNull()` tests matter because a rule on a missing value is NULL, which a `when` treats as not matched: without them a dispute with no amount or no status would be called `valid`. Checking the status second also makes the later tests safe, since by then it is one of the four known values. An open dispute has no `resolved_date`, so the last comparison is NULL for it and it stays `valid`.
